title: Steering Blood Toward Air
endLine: Where air runs short, lung arteries narrow, sending blood to better-ventilated units.

scenes.tts: The first film ended on a cost. A unit short of air sends on blood low in oxygen, and the mix pays for it. Can the lung do anything about that unit?
scenes.narration: The first film ended on a cost. A unit short of air sends on blood low in oxygen, and the mix pays for it. Can the lung do anything about that unit?
scenes.caption: The first film ended on a cost. A unit short of air sends on blood low in oxygen, and the mix pays for it. Can the lung do anything about that unit?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 world and colour map without a reset. COLOUR BY CONCEPT, as before: BLUE = air, ventilation; RED = blood, perfusion; YELLOW = the oxygen the blood leaves with (and the question); GREY = lung outline and minor labels. New in this film: ORANGE = the muscle ring of a small lung artery (narrowing); WHITE = a pressure gauge. THE WORLD, kept all film: the grey rounded lung outline fills about 70% of the frame height. Inside it, three lung units in a row, drawn as in the first film (rounded BLUE-outlined alveolus box, BLUE air arrow entering from above, RED blood arrow entering from below). A shared RED inflow trunk enters from the lower left and branches to the three units; just below each unit its RED branch passes through an ORANGE ring (the small artery), relaxed and open at the start. Above the units, the three RED outflow streams join into one vein that leaves at the right, carrying YELLOW dots (oxygen content). A small 'schematic' tag sits at bottom right all film. On 'a unit short of air', the LEFT unit's BLUE arrow thins to a thread and its box dims; its outgoing RED stream carries only a few YELLOW dots, while the middle and right streams stay full. On 'the mix pays', where the streams join, the YELLOW dots in the shared vein visibly thin out. On the question, the LEFT unit pulses and white text appears across the top: 'Can the lung fight back?' Ambient motion: BLUE air pulses gently in time with breathing; RED dots flow continuously.
Title 'Steering Blood Toward Air' fades in above the lung for 2 s while the question text fades out. Breathing pulses and blood flow continue; the LEFT unit stays dim with its thin BLUE thread.

scenes.tts: In a working muscle, an arteriole short of oxygen widens and draws more blood. The lung's small arteries do the opposite. Where alveolar oxygen falls, they narrow. Blood leaves the poorly ventilated region instead of pooling in it.
scenes.narration: In a working muscle, an arteriole short of oxygen widens and draws more blood. The lung's small arteries do the opposite. Where alveolar oxygen falls, they narrow. Blood leaves the poorly ventilated region instead of pooling in it.
scenes.caption: In a working muscle, an arteriole short of oxygen widens and draws more blood. The lung's small arteries do the opposite. Where alveolar oxygen falls, they narrow. Blood leaves the poorly ventilated region instead of pooling in it.
scenes.visual: On 'working muscle', the lung slides to the right 60% of the frame and a small pink muscle block with one RED arteriole and its own ORANGE ring appears at left, labelled 'muscle'. On 'widens', that ring opens wider and more RED dots pour through it; tag 'low oxygen: widens'. On 'the opposite', the muscle block fades out and the lung slides back to full size. On 'they narrow', the ORANGE ring under the LEFT (poorly ventilated) unit tightens to about half its width; tag 'low oxygen: narrows'. On 'Blood leaves', RED dots in the inflow trunk now turn aside from the left branch and flow mostly into the middle and right branches; the left branch carries a thin trickle. No amounts implied.

scenes.tts: Follow the poorly ventilated unit. Its air is unchanged, but less blood reaches it. Ventilation over less perfusion is a larger ratio. So its low ratio is pushed back up. Its lost blood goes to better-ventilated units.
scenes.narration: Follow the poorly ventilated unit. Its air is unchanged, but less blood reaches it. Ventilation over less perfusion is a larger ratio. So its low ratio is pushed back up. Its lost blood goes to better-ventilated units.
scenes.caption: Follow the poorly ventilated unit. Its air is unchanged, but less blood reaches it. Ventilation over less perfusion is a larger ratio. So its low ratio is pushed back up. Its lost blood goes to better-ventilated units.
scenes.visual: Camera eases toward the LEFT unit, which fills about half the frame height; the other two units stay visible at right. Beside it, a large fraction appears: a BLUE bar labelled 'ventilation' over a RED bar labelled 'perfusion', with a tag 'ratio' (bar lengths schematic, no numbers). On 'Its air is unchanged', the BLUE thread and the BLUE bar pulse but keep their size. On 'less blood', the RED branch thins further at the ORANGE ring and the RED bar shrinks. On 'a larger ratio', a vertical pointer labelled 'ratio' on a short grey scale marked only 'low' and 'high' slides upward a modest step (it does not reach 'high'). On 'pushed back up', the pointer pulses. On 'better-ventilated units', the camera eases back out; the extra RED dots visibly enter the middle and right units, whose BLUE arrows are full.

scenes.tts: The classic experiment came in nineteen forty-six. Von Euler and Liljestrand ventilated anaesthetized cats by pump and recorded pulmonary arterial pressure. Ten and a half percent oxygen strongly raised it. Pure oxygen lowered it slightly.
scenes.narration: The classic experiment came in 1946. Von Euler and Liljestrand ventilated anaesthetized cats by pump and recorded pulmonary arterial pressure. Ten and a half percent oxygen strongly raised it. Pure oxygen lowered it slightly.
scenes.caption: The classic experiment came in 1946. Von Euler and Liljestrand ventilated anaesthetized cats by pump and recorded pulmonary arterial pressure. Ten and a half percent oxygen strongly raised it. Pure oxygen lowered it slightly.
scenes.visual: Same lung, now as the whole lung of an experiment: tag top left 'cat, 1946' and a small grey bellows labelled 'pump' feeding all three BLUE air arrows equally (the left unit's thread is restored to full; all ORANGE rings relax and fade to grey outlines with a small '?' beside the middle one: the vessels are not yet named as the cause). A large WHITE dial gauge labelled 'pulmonary artery pressure' clips onto the RED inflow trunk at left, needle at a middle 'baseline' mark (no numbers: schematic). A BLUE gas chip on the pump reads 'air'. On 'Ten and a half percent', the chip morphs to '10.5% oxygen', all three BLUE arrows pale, and the WHITE needle swings strongly up and holds high. On 'Pure oxygen', the chip morphs to '100% oxygen', the BLUE arrows brighten, and the needle drops to just below baseline.

scenes.tts: Nerves might cause such a rise. So they cut the vagus nerves and removed the stellate ganglia. If nerves carried the signal, the rise should vanish. Did it?
scenes.narration: Nerves might cause such a rise. So they cut the vagus nerves and removed the stellate ganglia. If nerves carried the signal, the rise should vanish. Did it?
scenes.caption: Nerves might cause such a rise. So they cut the vagus nerves and removed the stellate ganglia. If nerves carried the signal, the rise should vanish. Did it?
scenes.visual: On 'nerves', two GREY wires grow into the lung from the top left, labelled 'vagus nerves' and 'stellate ganglia', each with a faint travelling pulse. On 'cut', a snip mark breaks the vagus wire and its loose ends fall away; on 'removed', the stellate wire and its knot fade out. The gas chip switches back to '10.5% oxygen' and the BLUE arrows pale again. The WHITE needle is hidden behind a grey cover with a large '?'. Question card across the top in YELLOW: 'Does the rise vanish?'

Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question card 'Does the rise vanish?', the covered gauge with its '?', the cut nerve ends and the pale BLUE arrows. Only ambient motion: slow breathing pulses and RED dots flowing in the trunk. No other change.

scenes.tts: It did not; the rise survived. They concluded it was due, in part, to hypoxia acting directly on the vessels. Keep that hedge. A pressure is not a resistance unless flow and outflow pressure are known. Nor can whole-lung hypoxia test regional matching.
scenes.narration: It did not; the rise survived. They concluded it was due, in part, to hypoxia acting directly on the vessels. Keep that hedge. A pressure is not a resistance unless flow and outflow pressure are known. Nor can whole-lung hypoxia test regional matching.
scenes.caption: It did not; the rise survived. They concluded it was due, in part, to hypoxia acting directly on the vessels. Keep that hedge. A pressure is not a resistance unless flow and outflow pressure are known. Nor can whole-lung hypoxia test regional matching.
scenes.visual: On 'the rise survived', the question card dissolves, the cover lifts and the WHITE needle is high, as before the cut. On 'acting directly on the vessels', the three grey ring outlines turn ORANGE and tighten slightly together; tag beside them 'in part: direct'. On 'Keep that hedge', the tag 'in part' brightens. On 'not a resistance', a small WHITE tag 'pressure is not resistance' attaches to the gauge, and two small grey '?' marks appear on the trunk and on the outflow vein, labelled 'flow?' and 'outflow pressure?'. On 'whole-lung hypoxia', all three units pale together and a tag reads 'whole lung, not regions'.

scenes.tts: Still, their proposal is the idea to carry. Where a region runs short of oxygen, its small arteries narrow. Blood shifts toward the better aerated parts. That is the lung's local correction for mismatch.
scenes.narration: Still, their proposal is the idea to carry. Where a region runs short of oxygen, its small arteries narrow. Blood shifts toward the better aerated parts. That is the lung's local correction for mismatch.
scenes.caption: Still, their proposal is the idea to carry. Where a region runs short of oxygen, its small arteries narrow. Blood shifts toward the better aerated parts. That is the lung's local correction for mismatch.
scenes.visual: The experiment props fade (cat tag, pump, cut nerves, gauge, '?' marks, tags). The lung returns to the opening picture: the LEFT unit's BLUE arrow is again a thin thread, the middle and right units fully ventilated, all ORANGE rings relaxed. On 'runs short of oxygen', the LEFT unit dims. On 'narrow', only the LEFT ring tightens. On 'Blood shifts', RED dots reroute from the left branch into the middle and right branches. On 'local correction', a large label appears over the lung: 'less oxygen here, less blood', with a thin arrow to the LEFT unit.

scenes.tts: How does a vessel respond to low oxygen? In outline, hypoxia inhibits an outward potassium current in the artery's smooth muscle. The cell depolarizes, and voltage-gated calcium channels open. That is one route among several.
scenes.narration: How does a vessel respond to low oxygen? In outline, hypoxia inhibits an outward potassium current in the artery's smooth muscle. The cell depolarizes, and voltage-gated calcium channels open. That is one route among several.
scenes.caption: How does a vessel respond to low oxygen? In outline, hypoxia inhibits an outward potassium current in the artery's smooth muscle. The cell depolarizes, and voltage-gated calcium channels open. That is one route among several.
scenes.visual: Camera dives into the LEFT unit's ORANGE ring until one smooth muscle cell fills about 65% of the frame height: a long ORANGE rounded block, labelled 'smooth muscle cell'. Labelled-block cartoon only, no molecular structures. On its upper edge, a door labelled 'potassium current' lets small grey dots stream outward; on 'inhibits', the door swings mostly shut and the outward stream slows to a few dots. On 'depolarizes', a simple WHITE meter on the cell labelled 'membrane voltage' swings toward less negative. On 'calcium channels open', two doors on the lower edge labelled 'calcium channels' open and small PURPLE dots flow in; the ORANGE block shortens and thickens. On 'one route among several', a tag 'one route of several' appears, with two faint unlabelled side arrows into the cell.

scenes.tts: The sensor upstream is still hypothesized; mitochondria are the leading candidate. In mice lacking one mitochondrial subunit, Cox four i two, isolated lungs did not constrict to hypoxia. They constricted normally to potassium chloride.
scenes.narration: The sensor upstream is still hypothesized; mitochondria are the leading candidate. In mice lacking one mitochondrial subunit, Cox4i2, isolated lungs did not constrict to hypoxia. They constricted normally to potassium chloride.
scenes.caption: The sensor upstream is still hypothesized; mitochondria are the leading candidate. In mice lacking one mitochondrial subunit, Cox4i2, isolated lungs did not constrict to hypoxia. They constricted normally to potassium chloride.
scenes.visual: Inside the same ORANGE cell, a CYAN bean-shaped mitochondrion fades in near the potassium door with a large '?' and the label 'sensor? (hypothesized)'. Camera pulls back out to the lung, now tagged at top left 'isolated mouse lung'; a small CYAN bean icon with a white cross sits beside the LEFT ring, labelled 'Cox4i2 removed'. Two large test buttons appear below the lung. On 'did not constrict to hypoxia', the button 'hypoxia' lights, the BLUE arrows pale, and the LEFT ORANGE ring stays open (a WHITE cross beside it). On 'potassium chloride', the button 'potassium chloride' lights and the same ring tightens normally (a WHITE tick beside it).

scenes.tts: So the contraction machinery works. In mouse lungs, the defect sits upstream, in sensing or its signaling. In humans, the sensor remains an open question.
scenes.narration: So the contraction machinery works. In mouse lungs, the defect sits upstream, in sensing or its signaling. In humans, the sensor remains an open question.
scenes.caption: So the contraction machinery works. In mouse lungs, the defect sits upstream, in sensing or its signaling. In humans, the sensor remains an open question.
scenes.visual: The test buttons fold into a chain of three large boxes across the lower third, left to right, joined by arrows: 'sensing' (CYAN) to 'signaling' to 'contraction' (ORANGE). On 'machinery works', 'contraction' gets a WHITE tick. On 'defect sits upstream', a WHITE bracket spans 'sensing' and 'signaling' labelled 'defect here (mouse)'; neither box is singled out. On 'In humans', the bracket's label gains a second line 'humans: open question' and the CYAN '?' returns on the 'sensing' box.

scenes.tts: In healthy lungs at rest, on air at sea level, the response does little. It matters when ventilation becomes uneven between regions, or at altitude.
scenes.narration: In healthy lungs at rest, on air at sea level, the response does little. It matters when ventilation becomes uneven between regions, or at altitude.
scenes.caption: In healthy lungs at rest, on air at sea level, the response does little. It matters when ventilation becomes uneven between regions, or at altitude.
scenes.visual: The chain fades; the full lung returns, mouse tag gone. On 'healthy lungs at rest', all three BLUE arrows are full and equal, all ORANGE rings relaxed and still; tag 'healthy, rest, sea level: little'. On 'uneven between regions', the LEFT BLUE arrow thins to its thread and only the LEFT ring tightens. On 'at altitude', a small grey mountain icon with the tag 'altitude' appears at top right, and all three BLUE arrows pale slightly together. No amounts implied.

scenes.tts: So a spread of ratios is not left alone. A region short of air gives up part of its blood, and its ratio rises. Blood is steered toward units with air.
scenes.narration: So a spread of ratios is not left alone. A region short of air gives up part of its blood, and its ratio rises. Blood is steered toward units with air.
scenes.caption: So a spread of ratios is not left alone. A region short of air gives up part of its blood, and its ratio rises. Blood is steered toward units with air.
scenes.visual: The mountain fades; the lung is back to the opening picture with the LEFT unit short of air. On 'gives up part of its blood', the LEFT ORANGE ring tightens and its RED branch thins (not to zero); the small 'low / high' ratio pointer from s03 reappears beside the LEFT unit and slides up a modest step. On 'steered toward units with air', RED dots stream into the middle and right units, whose full BLUE arrows pulse together. The YELLOW dots in the shared vein are left unchanged (no amount claimed).

End card over the dimmed but still moving lung (breathing pulses, RED dots flowing mostly through the middle and right branches, LEFT ring narrowed). Large centred white text: 'Where air runs short, lung arteries narrow, sending blood to better-ventilated units.'
